c: A gap in a treatment that was working can quickly undo its benefit. Here is what the evidence does and does not show, and how to plan for continuity.
When an ADHD medicine that was helping stops, symptoms can return quickly. In the selected adult responders studied below, most relapses after switching to placebo occurred within two weeks. A
break, agreed with a clinician and reviewed, is different from an
gap caused by a broken pathway. The aim of this page is to help you get a timely, reasoned decision either way.

Why does benefit fade so fast? Stimulants act within hours and are cleared within hours; they do not "build up" a lasting store of benefit. So stopping removes the effect on the next day's symptoms, not months later.
Why might harms follow? Large registry studies show that people with ADHD who

medication have lower rates of several serious outcomes than similar people who do not start. Those studies are about starting, not stopping — but they explain why clinicians and patients take unmet need seriously.

a.aria-label: Research finding, confidence strong: show sources

c: Among 148,578 people in Sweden newly diagnosed with ADHD, starting medication within three months was associated with lower two-year all-cause mortality (39.1 vs 48.1 per 10, 000; HR 0.79), driven by unnatural causes such as injuries, poisoning and suicide.

c: In a matching analysis, starting treatment was associated with fewer first episodes of suicidal behaviour (IRR 0.83), substance misuse, transport accidents and criminality — but not accidental injuries — with larger reductions in people who had had previous events.

What these studies do not show

They compare people who started treatment with people who did not. They do not measure what happens when an established, working treatment is withdrawn, and their numbers should not be reversed into an estimate of withdrawal harm. They support concern and planning — not a calculated risk for any individual.
Before or during any gap, get these five answers in writing. The
has a request you can build and copy.
Who will make the next prescribing decision?
What records of previous benefit and side effects will they receive?
What checks or reassessment are needed, and who arranges them?
What is the interim plan and review date, and what happens if function deteriorates?
If shared care is not accepted, who supplies the medicine?
NICE asks that medication review include the effects of missed doses, planned dose reductions and periods of no treatment, and that the reasons for continuing are documented.

A restart after a gap is a clinical decision, not an administrative one. It should weigh the documented previous benefit, the reasons the gap happened, current physical and mental health, and the safest way to re-establish the dose. See

In one case, a trust declined a "bridging" prescription on the grounds that restarting at the previous dose after several weeks off, outside an active treatment plan, would not be safe without a new assessment and titration plan.
That reasoning is common and can be legitimate. The question it leaves is
: if reassessment is required, who provides it, and how soon?

Interruption has several common causes in the UK, none controlled by the patient: national supply shortages; GP practices declining shared care (which places responsibility back with the specialist); discharge without a receiving prescriber; prescription lengths that do not match re-order rules; and substitution between products. Each produces a gap through a different broken link — and each needs a different fix.
Ministers have said GP practices may decline shared care, with responsibility then remaining with the specialist service.
The independent ADHD Taskforce found ADHD under-recognised and under-treated in England.
